title: API Reference
markdown:
The FastAPI surface lives in `openexecutive.api.main`, which mounts one router per topic. A shared-secret middleware gates every request via an `x-api-key` header, except `/health` and the `/webhook/*` callbacks (which carry their own verification). With local login (`OE_LOCAL_LOGIN=1`, which only `make dev` sets, and only while neither Google nor SSO sign-in is set up) a second middleware answers 403 to any request whose raw `Host` is not `localhost`, `127.0.0.1` or `[::1]` (except a webhook that verifies its caller: Google Chat and Slack always, Telegram only with a `TELEGRAM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` Telegram can send), and to any write whose `Sec-Fetch-Site` is present and not `same-origin`/`none`. The UI signs that owner in with no password and this API usually has no secret, so without it a web page in the owner's browser could drive the API as the principal — by DNS-rebinding its own hostname to 127.0.0.1, or by posting a plain form from another site or localhost port. CORS is restricted to the UI origins in `BACKEND_ALLOWED_ORIGINS`, plus the `make dev` UI on `localhost:3000` only when `OE_PUBLIC_DEPLOYMENT` is unset, so a public instance never answers a localhost page with credentials. The gate is off when `BACKEND_SHARED_SECRET` is unset — intended for local development only — so any internet-reachable deployment sets `OE_PUBLIC_DEPLOYMENT`, and `create_app()` then refuses to boot without the secret rather than serving an unauthenticated API.

**Who is calling** is read in one place, `api/caller.py`, which answers with a `Caller` kind and email; a test fails on any other read of an `x-caller-*` header. By default (`open`) it is the `x-caller-email` the UI proxy stamps from the sign-in, trusted because whoever holds the shared secret is trusted as the proxy, and a request with none runs as the principal. **Signed callers** remove that trust. With `CALLER_ASSERTION_PUBLIC_KEYS` set, the proxy signs every request with an Ed25519 key only the UI holds, and a third middleware checks the `x-caller-assertion` header:

- **What it covers.** It is good for one method, the exact path and query, at most 120 seconds, and one use. The API keeps used ids in memory.
- **What it names.** A `user`, by email, or the `operator`: local login, which runs as the principal.
- **No caller header at all** is a `service`, for scripts or MCP clients holding only the secret. It is never the principal, not even on an install with no owner yet, so it can't save a first setup.
- **Anything else is a 401.** That includes an `x-caller-email` without an assertion (`caller_assertion_required`), and a bad, expired, reused or mismatched assertion (`caller_assertion_invalid`).

Public keys that can't be read stop the boot, rather than fall back to trusting the header. `scripts/make-caller-keys.py` makes the pair, and `scripts/mint-caller-assertion.py` signs one request for curl. The API holds only public keys. Setup's API-protection check warns while a shared secret is set without them.

Endpoints grouped by router:

| Router | Key endpoints | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `chat` | `POST /chat`, `POST /chat/stop`, `POST /chat/add`, `POST /chat/background` | SSE stream of a live Executive turn, with a `: keepalive` comment every `CHAT_STREAM_KEEPALIVE_S` while the turn is quiet. `POST /chat/background` starts a new chat that the server answers to the end with nobody connected (a phone approving a card, then closing the app): it answers `202` with the new `session_id` once the same caller, access and quota checks as `/chat` pass, the turn saves itself as a `/chat` turn does, and one caller may have three running at once (`429` beyond that). `POST /chat/add` hands the running turn a message the person typed while it works; the turn takes it at its next step and the stream names it in a `message_added` event, and a second `POST /chat` on the same conversation waits for the first to finish. The request body optionally carries `page_context` (route, page title, guide section id, and a form descriptor with current values) — sent only by the Ask OE side panel so the Executive can explain the current page or propose form values. When the Executive calls its `propose_form_values` tool, the stream emits a `form_patch` event (`{type, form_id, fields, rationale, iteration}`) that the panel applies into the on-screen form as highlighted suggestions; the user reviews and saves through the form's normal submit path. Each round of tool calls also emits an `activity` event (`{type, label, tool, iteration}`) naming what is running — progress only, forwarded verbatim and never persisted with the message, unlike an `action_taken` chip. A `session_id` in the body must be a chat the caller may use (the same ownership rule as `sessions`). If it isn't, the turn runs in a fresh chat instead, so nothing is written into someone else's session and the reply looks the same as for an unknown id. An unknown namespaced id (`slack:…`, `telegram:…` and so on) is ignored and a fresh chat is started, because those ids belong to the channel adapters and claiming one first would make the caller its owner. The client mints a `client_turn_id` and sends it with the turn; `POST /chat/stop` takes that id and halts the turn mid-flight, so the button is live from the moment Send is pressed rather than only once the first SSE byte arrives. A stopped turn emits a `stopped` event and then the usual `done` over the same still-open stream — never an `error` — and whatever streamed so far is persisted and flagged. The endpoint returns 404 both for an unknown id and for another caller's turn, so it cannot be used to probe which turns are live. An optional `memory_text` (1–2000 chars) is what peer memory records as the caller's words instead of `message` — the briefing handoffs send it because their seed quotes the Executive's own card; `POST /chat/upload` derives it from the typed text and filenames. Since it never reaches the transcript, the `chat_turn` audit row keeps it beside `message`. After the reply — a stopped or timed-out one too, before the `stopped` / `error` / `done` frames — a turn that looked at anything sends one `sources` event, `{type, session_id, sources: [{kind, title, url}], unavailable: [area]}`: `kind` is `company`, `knowledge`, `notion`, `research`, `document` or `web`, `url` is only ever an http(s) link or, for an earlier document, `/artifacts/<id>`, at most 12 sources (6 from the web, pages the reply cites first), and `unavailable` names parts of the analysis ("finance") whose specialist failed or said nothing every time it was asked. It is persisted with the reply as `chat_messages.sources`. A request that carries `x-caller-email` marks its turn signed in (`Session.web_caller_signed_in`), which Act as me needs on a deployment without local login. |
| `sessions` | `GET /sessions`, `GET /sessions/shared-with-me`, `GET\|PATCH /sessions/{id}`, `GET /sessions/{id}/messages`, `DELETE /sessions/{id}`, `POST /sessions/{id}/messages/{message_id}/feedback`, `GET /sessions/{id}/followup`, `GET\|PUT /sessions/{id}/shares`, `DELETE /sessions/{id}/shares/me`, `GET /sessions/{id}/people`, `GET /sessions/{id}/live`, `POST /sessions/{id}/typing`, `GET /sessions/{id}/export`, `POST /sessions/{id}/rewind` | List, read and delete saved chat sessions (assistant messages carry their row `id` and any `feedback`). The list is scoped to the caller, and each chat carries `preview`: its last message as one plain line, Markdown marks stripped and cut at a word near 120 characters, with `You:` before the person's own words. With `?q=` it is a search: the caller's own chats whose title or message text contains the words (case-insensitive, `LIKE` with wildcards escaped), each with `match_count` (messages that contain them; 0 for a title-only match) and `snippet` (the newest matching message, around the match, prefixed `You:` or `Executive:`). Scoped exactly like the list, so nobody else's conversation can match. The Chats page searches this way and opens a result with `?find=`, so the chat starts on that message and steps through the others. A chat-app conversation started with /new is left off the list until its first turn (`memory.conversations`). Every per-session route checks ownership, because session ids are guessable (`slack:dm:<user id>`, `telegram:<chat id>`): only the session's owner or the principal gets through, and a legacy row with no owner is the principal's alone. A teammate's own chat (a web chat, a DM, a private Telegram chat; not a channel or group conversation, `chat._shared_space`) is theirs alone, the principal included, as their mail with the Executive is. Anyone else gets the same 404 as for an unknown id, so the routes can't be used to find out which chats exist. The one other way in is having started the chat in this process (matched by Person id or verified email, so it survives the caller being added to the roster), which is how a caller the roster can't resolve keeps using their own chat. That record is in memory, so after a restart such an ownerless chat is refused for reads. The principal can continue someone else's ownerless chat without becoming its owner. Deleting a session also drops its in-memory copy, so a later turn naming that id starts fresh. The feedback route records 👍/👎 (`{"feedback": "up"|"down"|null}`) on one assistant reply; only the session's own caller or the principal may rate it. The rater is stored (`feedback_by_person_id`), and a 👎 on a reply to the rater's own message triggers a working-style pass for them (paced; see attunement). The chat stream's `done` event carries `message_id` for the persisted reply. The followup route returns `{"suggestion": string|null}` — one suggested next user message, written by the utility-fast model from the last few turns, that the chat composer shows as its greyed placeholder (Tab / → or the inline chip fills it in without sending). It is null unless the session ends on a persisted assistant reply, and null (uncached) when the model fails. Same ownership check as feedback; successful suggestions are cached in-process per (session, reply id). Messages from `GET /sessions/{id}/messages` carry each assistant reply's saved `sources` (the same shape as the chat stream's `sources` event, without `type`), so a reloaded chat shows them again. The owner (not the principal on someone else's chat; the principal for an ownerless one) also has the chat controls. `PATCH` takes `{title?, pinned?}`: a name they give is kept (`sessions.title_locked`, so the automatic title never replaces it) and a pinned chat lists first, newest pin first, with `pinned_at`. `PUT /sessions/{id}/shares {person_ids}` adds exactly those team members to it (not contacts, the archived or the owner: 422), audited `session_shared`; a chat that read its owner's own mail (`mail_private`) is never shared (409) and stops being open to those it was shared with before, and a chat-app conversation is never shared (409). Those added get it from `GET /sessions/shared-with-me` (with `shared_with_you`, `shared_by`, `shared_at`) and **write in it with the owner**: `POST /chat` with its id runs their turn as themselves (`chat._shared_member` widens the turn's access, never its ownership), and they may read it, its messages (without the owner's ratings) and its export. They can't rate, rename, delete, share or redo it, and `DELETE /sessions/{id}/shares/me` takes them out of it (audited `session_shared`, with them under `removed`). In a chat several people are in, messages carry `sender_person_id` and `sender_name` (a message from before it was shared is the owner's), `GET /sessions/{id}/people` returns `{you, people: [{person_id, full_name, owner}]}` (owner first; empty for a chat of one), and redo is refused (409) when the last message is someone else's. `GET /sessions/{id}/live` is a server-sent event stream each open page holds (`api.chat_live`, one in-process broker): `ready` first (with the running turn so far, if any), then `turn_started` (who sent what), the reply's `chunk` / `thinking` / `activity` / `action_taken` / `phase`, `turn_ended` (the page reads the chat again), `typing` (from `POST /sessions/{id}/typing`, at most once per 2 s per person) and `people`. `removed`, `deleted` and `resync` (a page that fell 1024 events behind) end it; the access check runs again on every 20 s keepalive. At most 12 pages per person, 40 per chat and 2000 per process (429). Archiving someone takes them out of every chat shared with them, and their open streams close at the next keepalive. The page closes it while its tab is hidden. `GET /sessions/{id}/export` returns the chat as a Markdown file (`memory.chat_export`: each message under its writer's People name or `Executive`, the reply's sources listed under it). `POST /sessions/{id}/rewind {last_message_id}` takes back the last turn for Try again and Edit: under the conversation's turn lock it deletes the last reply and the messages it answered, but only while that reply is still the chat's last row, and returns those messages' words (`{message}`), which the page sends again as an ordinary `/chat` turn through the usual gates. 409 while a turn is answering, for a stale reply id, and for a chat-app conversation (its reply also lives in Slack, Telegram or Discord); audited `session_rewound`. |
| `today` | `GET /today`, `GET /today/activity`, `GET /today/activity/daily`, `GET /today/brief-delivery`, `GET /today/value`, `GET /today/top-three`, `GET /today/weekly-review` | Morning-brief aggregation, recent-action rail, Pulse heartbeat heatmap (per-day activity counts), and the owner's Your month tally (`GET /today/value?period=month|week&offset=N`: counted lines beside the period before plus the finished reports, owner only, 403 otherwise; see Today). `GET /today` carries the viewer's cached "What's going on" `narrative` with `narrative_generated_at` (when it was written) and `narrative_stale` (a fresher one is being written — the page re-polls; see Today). A proposal backed by a roster request carries `roster_request` (the new sender's server-derived details and held-message previews; the principal's only) and is answered through the `people` routes below. `brief-delivery` returns the latest morning brief or end-of-day digest that didn't reach the owner, as `{brief, at, problem, fix, readable}` in plain language (`readable` is false when it couldn't be written, so there is nothing to read), or null — null while briefs go out, once the cause is fixed, while the scheduler is off, and for anyone but the owner (`chat._caller_is_principal_or_unclaimed`); it carries no address or channel id. `top-three` and `weekly-review` feed the solo Briefing's own cards and answer only in solo mode and only to the principal (`workflows._caller_is_the_principal`: a principal match or no caller header, never an unclaimed roster); anyone else, and team mode, get null. `top-three` returns `{items: [{key, kind, text, why, slot}]}` — the morning brief's top three from the same code (`build_top_three(principal_due_soon())`), `slot` a free block like `10:00–11:00`, `""` when none is left, null when no calendar was read — and is kept off `GET /today` because its calendar read may take up to 4 s. `weekly-review` returns the latest completed `weekly_review` run as `{run_id, completed_at, period, top_three, excerpt}` (next week's top three as plain text; `excerpt` when that list is empty), or null when none has completed. |
| `people` | `GET\|POST\|PATCH /people`, `POST /people/{id}/archive`, `GET /people/requests`, `GET /people/requests/{id}`, `POST /people/requests/{id}/approve`, `POST /people/requests/{id}/decline`, `GET\|POST /people/{id}/open-loops` (a `POST` tells the owner once and returns `notified`: `sent` with the channel, `held`, `not_reached` or `skipped`; see Attunement), `POST /open-loops/{loop_id}/close`, `GET /people/{id}/outreach`, `GET\|PUT\|DELETE /people/{id}/attunement` | Roster CRUD and scope lookups. Every `Person` carries `kind` (`team` / `contact`). `GET /people` lists team members only unless `?include_contacts=true` (the People page asks for both; the department-head and workflow pickers keep the default); `POST` / `PATCH` accept `kind`, and a principal contact is a 422 either way. They also take `email_aliases` (other addresses the person writes from, at most 10; on `PATCH` the full list replaces the current one, omitted leaves it): an alias matches their mail and may be emailed but never signs in; a malformed one is a 422, and an alias — or a new primary `email` — that is already someone else's address or alias is a 409. Every `POST` / `PATCH` then closes any pending roster request whose sender now matches someone and replays its held messages. Adding, editing and archiving (`POST`, `PATCH`, `/archive`) are the principal's only, or anyone's while no one is principal yet so a first setup can add its owner (`chat._caller_is_principal_or_unclaimed`, the check behind `PUT /workspace`; a request with no `x-caller-email`, such as the CLI or local login, counts as the principal). Anyone else, a person editing their own row included, gets 403 before the person lookup, so it can't probe which ids exist. Contacts are private to the principal (`caller_is_principal`: the signed-in email is the principal's, or no `x-caller-email`; stricter than the owner rule above, so while no one is principal nobody is): for anyone else `include_contacts` is ignored, a contact's id is a 404 on `GET /people/{id}` and open-loops (exactly as for a missing id; `PATCH` and archive are already a 403 for them), and creating a contact or turning someone into one is a 403, even on a first setup with no principal yet. `GET /people/me` returns `{person_id, is_principal}` so the UI offers contacts to the principal only. `GET /people/by-scope/{token}` never returns a contact. Archiving a person closes their open loops. The open-loop routes list what a person owes (soonest due first) and close one (`reason`: done / not_needed / cancelled) — both the principal's or the owner's only (403 otherwise, via `people.store.is_principal_or_self`). `POST /people/{id}/open-loops` `{task, due_date?}` assigns that person a task (201 with the loop; `due_date` is a local date, due 17:00 in the user's timezone, clamped to 60 days, default 2 days): any active team member may assign anyone on the team, 403 for anyone else; 409 for an archived person, a contact (as seen by the principal), a person at the open-loop cap, a duplicate or open loops turned off; 422 for an empty task. Nobody is messaged at assignment — the owner is chased once it is due. `/outreach` returns, per kind of proactive outreach over 30 days, `sent` / `replied` / `acted` / `ignored` / `pending` (voided DMs are excluded) — same access rule, checked before the person lookup so it can't probe which ids exist. `/attunement` reads, replaces (`rules`: up to 4 strings, or omitted to only set `locked`) or resets the person's working-style rules — same access rule, 404 for an archived person; `PUT` rejects a rule that is not purely about style with 422. Archiving a person also drops their working style and frees their aliases. The **roster-request** routes (declared before `/people/{person_id}`) are the principal's alone (`caller_is_principal`; anyone else gets 404, as for a missing id): `GET /people/requests?status=pending|approved|linked|declined|expired|superseded|all` lists up to 100 (`id`, `channel`, `channel_ref`, sanitised `display_name`, `profile_email`, `on_company_domain`, `suggested_kind`, `suggested_person_id` / `_name`, `status`, `resolved_person_id` / `_kind`, `message_count`, timestamps, `ack_sent`, and `previews` of the held messages while pending — shown to the principal, never to a model); `approve` takes either `link_person_id` (+ `replace_channel_id`) or `full_name` + `kind` (no default: 422 without both) + optional `role`; `decline` takes no body. An answered request is a 409, a chat id or address already on someone else is a 409; the held messages are replayed (or dropped) in the background. |
| `departments` | `GET\|POST\|PATCH\|DELETE /departments`, `.../goals` | Department state and per-department goals. `PATCH /departments/{slug}` also takes `watched_entities` (≤50 names, `[]` clears) — the entities the research watch policy may add watches for and route to this department. A `cadences` spec that does not parse is rejected with a 422 (empty means no cadence, i.e. the check-in is off); a changed `check_in` cancels the pending check-in and queues the next one on the new schedule. `GET` and `PATCH /departments/{slug}` return the department state plus `next_check_in_at` (ISO UTC of the pending check-in, `null` when it is off, the workspace is solo or none is queued); the list route does not carry it. A new `head_person_id` must be a team member: an unknown id and one of the principal's contacts get the same name-free 422 (`person_id N is not on the team.`), so the route — open to any signed-in user — never reveals that a contact exists; an unchanged head is not re-checked. `POST .../goals` requires only `key_result`: a missing or blank `period_value` is filled with the current period for `period_type` in the user's zone (the same label `create_goal` uses), and `target` defaults to empty. `PATCH .../goals/{id}` rejects a blank `key_result` or `period_value` with a 422; `target` may be cleared. |
| `agents` | `GET /agents`, `GET /agents/models`, `GET /agents/models/options`, `GET /agents/presets`, `POST /agents/presets/{id}`, `PATCH /agents/{id}`, `POST /agents/{id}/test` | Specialist metadata and Council overrides. `/agents/models` is the flat model allowlist the PATCH validator uses; `/agents/models/options` returns the same ids in the same order, each tagged with `provider`, `provider_label`, `route` (`direct` / `openrouter` / `local`) and a display `label`, for the Council's Provider → Model picker. `AgentDetail` carries `instructions` (additional instructions, appended after `prompt`, which stays the built-in prompt or its replacement); `PATCH` and `/test` accept `instructions` (max 4,000 chars, blank clears it). `GET /agents/presets` lists the Fast, Balanced and Thorough quality presets (each with `available` and the resolved `model` for this install) plus `active` (null when the council is Custom), `base` and `custom_agents`; `POST /agents/presets/{id}` applies one by writing per-agent model and deep-reasoning overrides and returns the same shape (404 unknown preset, 409 when the install allows none of its models). Each `AgentMeta` carries `visibility` (`core` or `internal`) so the Council's simple view can list core agents first. |
| `personas` | `GET\|PUT\|POST\|DELETE /personas` | Executive persona definitions. |
| `alerts` | `POST /alerts/{id}/approve`, `GET /alerts/approvals/{id}`, `POST /alerts/{id}/ack`, `POST /alerts/bulk-ack`, `POST /alerts/{id}/snooze`, `POST /alerts/{id}/reopen`, `POST /alerts/review` | Groom the briefing queue. `approve` (body `{edited_body?}`, 202) carries a proposal card out on the server and records who approved it and when (`alerts.approvals`, see Today): it queues the scheduled action a department-gated card held, or runs one Executive turn as the approver in a new chat (`session_id`). 409 for a card already approved or closed, a decision-backed card (approved at `/decisions`), a roster request or a drafted artifact; 403 unless the caller is the card's routed person or the principal (an unrouted card is the principal's); 429 when the caller already has three background turns running. `GET /alerts/approvals/{id}` reads one back (`running`, then `done` / `failed` with `outcome`) for its approver, the card's person or the principal (404 for anyone else). `snooze` (`until`, an ISO time up to 30 days ahead; `null` clears it, the Undo) hides an `unread` card until then by setting `snoozed_until` (409 on a closed card or a roster request); the TTL then counts from the snooze, so a card snoozed past its TTL still comes back. `ack` (`read`/`ack`/`dismissed`, optional `mute_topic`) also teaches a watch-sourced alert's watch (`trust_score`); `bulk-ack` takes explicit `alert_ids` and/or `older_than_days` + `category` (exempt sources skipped); `reopen` is the Undo for a `resolved` / `expired` / `dismissed` alert (never `ack` or an artifact / decision row; back to `unread` with every review stamp cleared and its TTL anchor refreshed, so it is live again even if older than its TTL); `review` runs the Executive's relevance review on demand (ignores the interval; still honours `ALERT_REVIEW_ENABLED`, the per-pass caps, the single-flight lock and per-alert idempotency) and returns the move counts. `bulk-ack` caps ids at 500, needs `older_than_days >= 1`, and applies watch feedback per row; `mute_topic` must be one of the alert's tags or a scoped `external:` / `department:` pattern. Alerts still surface only through the briefing (`/today` reads the live view) — there is no list, prefs, mutes, or live-stream endpoint. |
| `artifacts` | `GET /artifacts`, `GET /artifacts/{id}`, `GET /artifacts/{id}/download?as=`, `POST /artifacts/{id}/archive`, `POST /artifacts/{id}/restore`, `DELETE /artifacts/{id}` | Browsable deliverables in any format — Markdown, HTML, Word, Excel, or a link into a connected app — with `format`, `downloads`, `external_url`, `supersedes_id` and, for an extension's kind of document, `collection` / `collection_label` on every summary (`orchestrator.extensions`; archive, restore and delete tell the collection first and answer 502 if it refuses). `download` renders the file (Word/Excel built at request time from the stored text; any Markdown artifact, workflow output included, can export `?as=docx`) and is always an attachment with `nosniff` and a sandbox CSP. Every route answers for the signed-in caller (`artifact_records.Viewer`): a drafted artifact is its owner's alone (`alerts.owner_person_id`, the person whose conversation published it; none = the principal's), a workflow output follows its run (`persistence.run_visible_to`), and anything the caller may not see is a 404 like a missing id, the principal included. `POST /alerts/{id}/ack` and `/reopen` answer 404 for someone else's drafted artifact the same way. |
| `decisions` | `GET /decisions`, `POST /decisions/{id}/{approve,reject,cancel}`, `GET`/`PUT /decisions/classes/meeting_scheduling`, `GET /audit/reliability` | Approval-gated decision instances (e.g. calendar bookings). What approve/reject/cancel do is per class (`DECISION_CLASSES`, one `DecisionClassSpec` each; meeting booking books on approve and deletes on cancel; `delegation_reply`, an inbox reply card, is its approver's alone (`approver_only`) — hidden from everyone else, the principal included when it is a team member's — sends its Gmail draft on approve and, after a reject, deletes the draft unless it was edited; `department_action`, a team member's chat send or edit their department held (see Org), is the principal's and its approver's alone (`principal_and_approver`), makes that exact call on approve and audits `department_action_done` / `_failed` / `_declined`), and an instance of a class with no spec gets 409 instead of being carried out as another. Only the principal, or the person the decision went to for approval (`approver_person_id`), may approve, reject or cancel it. Anyone else gets 403, and a decision nobody was asked about, or one private to the principal, is the principal's alone. The resolver is recorded as `resolver_person_id`, and a reject that loses the race to another answer is a 409. `GET /audit/reliability` is the principal's alone (403 otherwise), because it counts private decisions too. A proposed booking is surfaced on the briefing as a companion alert; approve/reject/cancel here also clear that alert. An approval whose caller resolves to the principal runs the booking inside `grant_contact_egress()`, so a meeting the principal proposed with a contact can be created. Such a booking's payload is marked `private`: it is proposed to the principal, left out of anyone else's `GET /decisions`, and a 404 for them on `GET /decisions/{id}` and every action route. Reviewed in the briefing — there is no separate proposals page. The class routes read and set how meetings are handled: both return `{decision_class: "meeting_scheduling", mode: "propose" \| "auto_execute"}` (default `propose`); the `PUT` body is `{mode}`, principal-only (403 otherwise, open before a principal exists — but then only `propose` can be set: `auto_execute` is a 409 until a non-archived principal is on the roster), 422 on any other mode, and a change writes a `decision_class_mode_changed` audit row. In solo mode the class mode decides a booking, and `auto_execute` applies only to a turn the principal started on a verified surface — any other turn gets a proposal. |
| `delegation` | `GET`/`PUT /delegation`, `GET`/`PUT`/`DELETE /delegation/voice`, `POST /delegation/voice/learn`, `POST /delegation/voice/describe`, `POST /delegation/voice/signature`, `PUT /delegation/inbox`, `POST /delegation/inbox/check`, `GET /delegation/replies`, `PUT /delegation/replies/{id}/text`, `GET /delegation/actions`, `PUT /delegation/handle-it`, `PUT /delegation/disclosure`, `PUT /delegation/training`, `DELETE /delegation/learned/{id}`, `GET /delegation/handled`, `PUT /delegation/team` | Act as me — the **caller's own** delegation only; nobody sets it for anyone else. The run stream adds a `progress` event (`step_id`, `summary`) while an action step uses tools. Each catalog entry (`WorkflowMeta`) carries `is_custom`, `background` (true for the system-run built-ins the UI files under “System”) and `quick` (true for a Quick workflow, one per playbook nothing else follows, named `quick_<playbook>`). The run endpoint streams SSE; its `awaiting_human` event carries `delivery` (`self` \| `sent` \| `suppressed` \| `alerted` \| `failed`) alongside `person_id` / `question` / `awaiting_until`, because the outbound guard or an unreachable approver means the question may never have been asked — a client must not render “waiting on them” for those. A paused run ends the stream with neither `done` nor `error`, so that `awaiting_human` frame carries `terminal: true` to say so explicitly, plus `resumable` — whether the run continues by itself once answered or stops at the gate. `GET /workflows/runs/{run_id}` returns the run row with the resume payload replaced by a small `resume_progress` summary (`gate_step_id`, `completed_step_ids`, or `null`): the payload holds every completed step's full text, and the run-detail page polls this endpoint while a run is unfinished. |

It accepts `general` in `domain_filter` for the same reason. `/search` applies the same review gate as `retrieve()` — withheld (pending or rejected) built-in, external and failure rows are dropped, so the panel never advertises knowledge the Executive cannot use; it degrades to unfiltered rather than failing if review state is unreadable. `POST /knowledge/builtin` refuses a name already held by shipped content, and `POST|DELETE /knowledge/failures` now register and deregister for review — without that a user-authored failure case study had no review row, so no SME decision could block it. |

The UI saves one with `POST /workflows/custom/{name}/save-edit` (`{session_id, definition}`): the server saves the session's own draft, never a client-sent body, and only when it equals the `definition` the user reviewed (a later message is a 409, so the click saves only what was shown); it re-validates it, keeps the stored on/off state, and writes only if the stored workflow is still the version the conversation opened on — otherwise 409, as it is for a session about another workflow or one with nothing drafted yet. **What it may do** (`api/routes/may_do.py`): `GET /what-it-may-do` is read-only. It returns `{paused, sections}`, three sections in order (`as_you`, `executive`, `departments`), each `{key, title, available, unavailable, notes, rows, footer, goes}`, and each row `{id, what, outcome, then, why, setting, items}`: `outcome` is `goes`, `waits`, `always_waits`, `drafts` or `off`, and `setting` names where to change it (`act_as_me`, `handle_it`, `take_the_lead`, `pause`, `department:<slug>`, or empty). `as_you` is the caller's own (`available` false, with why, when they can't have Act as me); `executive` is the principal's alone (`available` false for anyone else); `departments` is everyone's. Any team member on People may call it; a contact, someone not on People, or a request with no caller outside local login gets 403. See Delegation → What it may do.

**How far it goes as you** (`api/routes/delegation.py`): `PUT /delegation/reach` takes `{step}`, one of `off`, `when_asked`, `inbox`, `careful`, `balanced`, `bold`, `everything`, and answers the caller's delegation state as `GET /delegation` does. Going down turns the switches above the step off, highest first; going up runs each switch's own route in order (`PUT /delegation`, `PUT /delegation/inbox`, `PUT /delegation/handle-it`, `PUT /delegation/take-the-lead`), so the first refusal (409 `gmail_not_connected`, a signed sign-in missing, `in_training`, 403 for Everything when not the owner) stops it at a whole step. See Delegation → How far it goes as you.

**Take the lead** (`api/routes/take_the_lead.py`): `GET /take-the-lead` returns the As the Executive switch, its six Ask first switches (`{kind, label, hint, on}`, the hint a plain line on what each one catches), the company's rules, whether this server can tie a change to the owner (`available`), and whether the Executive is paused. `PUT /take-the-lead` takes `{enabled?, ask_first?}`, and `POST /take-the-lead/rules` / `DELETE /take-the-lead/rules/{id}` add or remove a company rule (`{kind: person|domain|words|amount, value}`, 422 on a bad one). All four are the principal's alone (403). Anything that lets more happen on its own (turning it on, turning an Ask first off, removing a rule) needs a caller the API can tie to them (`delegation.verified.caller_refusal`, else 409). `GET /today/activity` adds `took_the_lead` rows (what Take the lead did, named, not quoted) and, for the caller alone, `sent_as_you` rows for what Handle it for me sent as them. Under `/delegation`: `PUT /delegation/take-the-lead {enabled}` is Take the lead as you (the owner's only for now; turning it on turns Handle it for me on), and `GET|POST /delegation/take-the-lead/rules` and `DELETE …/rules/{id}` manage the caller's own rules. `HandleItOut` gains `lead` and `lead_available`. A `take_the_lead_action` decision is approved or rejected through the existing `/decisions/{id}/approve|reject`. Training: the response also carries `training` (In training: everything waits unless allowed), `learned` (`{id, label, feature, example, uses, created_at}`: what it was allowed, the edit kept as an example by field) and `suggested` (`{key, label, approvals}`); `PUT` takes `training?` too, and leaving training while on needs the same provable owner as turning it on. `POST /take-the-lead/learned {key}` allows a current suggestion (404 for anything else; provable owner), `DELETE /take-the-lead/learned/{id}` makes it ask first again. `learned` also lists the owner's own Act as me senders (`feature` `act_as_me`), never anyone else's, and Remove works on those too. On a `take_the_lead_action` card, `POST /decisions/{id}/approve` takes `edits.input` (the card's editable fields, 422 for any other; the principal's alone, 403 for an area approver) and `edits.allow: true` (a training card only, 422 otherwise; the principal from a provable request, 403 otherwise), finishing `approved_with_edit` when a field changed.
